% ============================================================
% 1.2 Historical Background
% ============================================================
\subsection{Historical Background}\label{sub:HistoricalEstimates}

A local smooth solution gives us a genuine Navier--Stokes history, but not yet a reason that history can cross every finite time.
The known theory has narrowed this gap by asking the same question at successively finer levels: what do the equations keep under control, and what can still escape that control?

The route begins with total kinetic energy and then follows the derivative activity hidden inside its dissipation.
When pointwise derivative control fails, continuation theory identifies the strength of bound that would suffice.
Local regularity and scale-critical criteria then force any possible failure into smaller and more concentrated regions of spacetime.
The results did not appear in exactly this order.
The order below follows the tightening of the problem: each result takes up the form of escape left by the last and narrows it again.

\divider{Leray's Energy Estimate}

The first quantity that survives for every finite time is kinetic energy.
For a smooth solution, pair the momentum equation with \(u\) and integrate over space.
Incompressibility makes nonlinear transport and pressure vanish from the total balance, while viscosity removes energy through spatial variation:
\[
  \lVert u(t)\rVert_{L^2}^{2}
  +2\nu\int_0^t\lVert\nabla u(s)\rVert_{L^2}^{2}\,ds
  =
  \lVert u_0\rVert_{L^2}^{2}.
\]
The velocity is controlled in \(L^2\) at each time, and the total gradient cost is controlled after integration over time.

Leray regularized the equations, obtained compactness, and passed a subsequence to a global weak solution.
Weak lower semicontinuity preserved the energy bound as an inequality in that limit \parencite{Leray1934}.
On every finite interval,
\[
  u\in L^\infty(0,T;L^2),
  \qquad
  \nabla u\in L^2(0,T;L^2).
\]
Leray's construction was the first global weak-existence result for the three-dimensional whole-space Cauchy problem.
It reaches every finite time, but only in a weak energy class in which smoothness and uniqueness are not known.

The two pieces of the estimate also carry different kinds of time control.
The kinetic energy is bounded at each instant.
The first derivative is only paid for in total over the interval.
The next question is whether that accumulated payment prevents the derivative from becoming arbitrarily large at an individual time.

\divider{The Enstrophy Problem}

For a divergence-free decaying field,
\[
  \lVert\nabla u\rVert_{L^2}^{2}
  =
  \lVert\omega\rVert_{L^2}^{2},
  \qquad
  \omega:=\nabla\times u.
\]
The squared \(L^2\) size of \(\omega\) is the enstrophy.
Leray's estimate bounds the area under its time graph:
\[
  \int_0^T\lVert\omega(t)\rVert_{L^2}^{2}\,dt<\infty.
\]
A finite area does not bound the height of the graph.
Very tall enstrophy peaks on very short intervals remain compatible with the energy inequality.

The vorticity equation shows why three dimensions leave room for such growth:
\[
  \partial_t\omega+(u\cdot\nabla)\omega
  =
  (\omega\cdot\nabla)u+\nu\Delta\omega.
\]
Transport carries vorticity with the fluid and viscosity diffuses it.
The term \((\omega\cdot\nabla)u\) stretches and tilts vortex lines through the surrounding velocity gradient.
It is absent from the corresponding two-dimensional enstrophy balance, but in three dimensions it has no fixed sign:
\[
  \frac12\frac{d}{dt}\lVert\omega\rVert_{L^2}^{2}
  +\nu\lVert\nabla\omega\rVert_{L^2}^{2}
  =
  \int_{\mathbb R^3}(\omega\cdot\nabla)u\cdot\omega\,dx.
\]
Viscosity still resists sharp variation, but the energy estimate does not show that it always defeats stretching point by point in time.

The problem has now moved above velocity size.
Energy cannot escape, yet the derivatives that determine classical smoothness might.
To know what has to be controlled, one first needs to know what bound would let the existing smooth solution continue.

\divider{Higher Sobolev Continuation}

That question is answered by the local well-posedness theory.
For \(s>5/2\), an \(H^s\) velocity field is continuously differentiable, so its transport field is spatially Lipschitz.
The standard Sobolev theory, built from the Fujita--Kato and Kato semigroup methods, uses viscous smoothing and product estimates to close a short-time iteration of the equation \parencite{FujitaKato1964,Kato1984}.
It produces a unique local solution whose lifespan has a positive lower bound on every bounded \(H^s\) ball.

Suppose a smooth solution exists on \([0,T)\) and
\[
  \sup_{0\leq t<T}
  \lVert u(t)\rVert_{H^s}
  \leq M
\]
for one \(s>5/2\).
Choose an actual time \(t_0<T\).
Local theory restarted from \(u(t_0)\) gives a lifespan depending only on \(s\), \(M\), and \(\nu\).
When \(t_0\) is close enough to \(T\), that lifespan crosses \(T\), and uniqueness makes the restarted solution the continuation of the same history.

The same bound controls \(\lVert\nabla u\rVert_{L^\infty}\).
Standard differentiated estimates then propagate every higher Sobolev norm already present in the smooth datum.
More generally, finiteness of
\[
  \int_0^T\lVert\nabla u(t)\rVert_{L^\infty}\,dt
\]
prevents higher derivatives from blowing up through \(T\).

Continuation theory has changed the question from an undefined loss of smoothness into a definite blow-up alternative.
If the maximal smooth time \(T_*\) were finite, no continuation-grade \(H^s\) norm could remain uniformly bounded as \(t\uparrow T_*\), and the accumulated Lipschitz norm would have to diverge.
The energy inequality does not supply either bound.
The next advance asks what it can still say locally around a point where continuation might fail.

\divider{Caffarelli\textendash Kohn\textendash Nirenberg Partial Regularity}

The Caffarelli--Kohn--Nirenberg theorem applies the local energy inequality on shrinking neighbourhoods of spacetime points.
For \(z_0=(x_0,t_0)\), let
\[
  Q_r(z_0)
  :=
  B_r(x_0)\times(t_0-r^2,t_0).
\]
Suitable weak solutions obey a local energy inequality on these parabolic cylinders.
Their epsilon-regularity argument shows that sufficiently small scale-invariant velocity and pressure quantities on \(Q_r(z_0)\) force regularity on a smaller cylinder.

At a singular point, the contrapositive applies at every scale.
Every sufficiently small cylinder centred there must retain a definite amount of scale-invariant concentration, because one cylinder below the threshold would already make the point regular.
A covering argument then confines the possible singular set to a set of zero one-dimensional parabolic Hausdorff measure \parencite{CaffarelliKohnNirenberg1982}.

This makes any possible failure extraordinarily sparse, but it does not make the singular set empty.
One point would still defeat global smoothness.
The local theory has also revealed what such a point must do: sustain concentration in both space and time through every shrinking parabolic neighbourhood.
That creates the need for a norm that measures spatial intensity and temporal persistence together.

\divider{Ladyzhenskaya\textendash Prodi\textendash Serrin Criteria}

The earlier Ladyzhenskaya\textendash Prodi\textendash Serrin criteria provide exactly that joint measurement.
They ask for
\[
  u\in L^p(0,T;L^q(\mathbb R^3)),
  \qquad
  \frac{2}{p}+\frac{3}{q}\leq1,
  \qquad
  q>3.
\]
The exponent \(q\) measures how sharply the velocity can concentrate in space, while \(p\) measures how long that concentration can persist.

The mechanism appears when the equation is estimated at one derivative.
For \(q>3\), interpolation and Young's inequality give
\[
  \frac{d}{dt}\lVert\nabla u\rVert_{L^2}^{2}
  +\nu\lVert\Delta u\rVert_{L^2}^{2}
  \leq
  C_{\nu,q}
  \lVert u\rVert_{L^q}^{\frac{2q}{q-3}}
  \lVert\nabla u\rVert_{L^2}^{2}.
\]
The mixed-norm condition makes the coefficient on the right integrable in time.
Gr\"onwall's inequality keeps enstrophy finite, and continuation carries the solution through \(T\) \parencite{Prodi1959,Serrin1962,Serrin1963,Ladyzhenskaya1967}.

At the equality
\[
  \frac{2}{p}+\frac{3}{q}=1,
\]
the mixed norm is unchanged by the Navier--Stokes scaling.
The criteria have reached the natural balance between concentration size and concentration duration.
Yet the exponent \(2q/(q-3)\) diverges as \(q\) decreases to \(3\).
The estimate covers every \(q>3\) and stops at the critical spatial endpoint \(q=3\).

\divider{The Escauriaza\textendash Seregin\textendash \v{S}ver{\'a}k Endpoint}

Under the Navier--Stokes rescaling
\[
  u_\lambda(x,t)
  :=
  \lambda u(\lambda x,\lambda^2t),
\]
the spatial \(L^3\) norm is unchanged:
\[
  \lVert u_\lambda(t)\rVert_{L^3}
  =
  \lVert u(\lambda^2t)\rVert_{L^3}.
\]
A suspected concentration can be magnified to unit scale without weakening the norm that measures it.
The endpoint question is whether a bounded \(L^\infty_tL^3_x\) norm can still coexist with a finite singular time.

Escauriaza, Seregin, and \v{S}ver{\'a}k proved that it cannot \parencite{EscauriazaSereginSverak2003}.
Their argument assumes a first singular time and rescales around the concentration.
Compactness produces a nontrivial ancient limiting solution with zero terminal trace and suitable spatial decay.
Backward uniqueness for its vorticity, followed by unique continuation, then forces the limiting solution to vanish identically, contradicting the concentration used to construct it.
Thus a Leray--Hopf weak solution remains regular through \(T\) whenever
\[
  u\in L^\infty(0,T;L^3(\mathbb R^3)).
\]

This endpoint theorem initially says that the critical norm cannot stay bounded near a finite maximal time.
It could still appear possible for the norm to rise along isolated times and repeatedly return below some fixed level.
For the smooth compactly supported initial data used in his whole-space theorem, Seregin ruled out that behaviour \parencite{Seregin2012}:
\[
  \lim_{t\uparrow T_*}
  \lVert u(t)\rVert_{L^3(\mathbb R^3)}
  =\infty
\]
whenever \(T_*<\infty\) is the maximal smooth time.
The critical concentration would have to leave every finite level and remain above it as the endpoint approached.

Seregin's theorem gives no rate for this divergence.
Tao later proved that, along infinitely many times approaching any finite maximal time, the \(L^3\) norm must exceed a positive power of a triple logarithm of the inverse time remaining \parencite{Tao2021Quantitative}.
These results sharply constrain what a finite-time singularity would have to do.
They do not produce an upper bound from \(u_0\), \(\nu\), and the equations that stops it from doing so.

\divider{Where the Problem Sits Today}

The remaining gap is visible in the scaling of the first global bound.
At corresponding times,
\[
  \lVert u_\lambda(t)\rVert_{L^3}
  =
  \lVert u(\lambda^2t)\rVert_{L^3},
  \qquad
  \lVert u_\lambda(t)\rVert_{L^2}^{2}
  =
  \lambda^{-1}\lVert u(\lambda^2t)\rVert_{L^2}^{2}.
\]
For \(\lambda>1\), this scaling compresses the field to the shorter length \(1/\lambda\), preserves its critical \(L^3\) size, and reduces its \(L^2\) energy by the factor \(1/\lambda\).
The global energy bound alone cannot place a scale-independent ceiling on the critical norm.

At smaller scales, gradients grow and viscous dissipation becomes stronger.
Nonlinear transport grows under the same scaling and can move activity into those gradients.
The unresolved estimate must compare these simultaneous effects along one evolving fluid, instead of observing either one in isolation.

A frequency-doubling picture makes the timing of the obstruction visible, though it is only a heuristic.
If the active frequency doubles from one stage to the next, the spatial scale halves and the parabolic time scale quarters.
Those time scales form a convergent geometric series.
Positive duration at every stage does not preclude infinitely many stages from fitting before a finite time.
This is the Zeno cascade picture.

The established theory has now narrowed a possible finite endpoint into a precise form.
Energy remains finite, but derivative activity would have to concentrate through every smaller parabolic scale, drive the critical \(L^3\) norm to infinity, and defeat every continuation-grade bound.
The classical results surveyed above do not supply an estimate generated by \(u_0\), \(\nu\), and the equations that stays uniform as the candidate endpoint is approached.
The next section examines what that direct estimate would have to pay.
